failure_modes: Assay sensitivity floor: particle counters, immuno-capture reagents, or spike-in tracer fail to detect low-biomass recovered material from lavage/CSF/tissue, producing false negatives attributed to senescence.

Spike-in tracer incompatibility: exogenous tracer behaves differently from endogenous EVs during fractionation, capture, or in vivo mucosal transit, invalidating recovery-normalization and masking true sample differences.

Capture reagent bias: antibody panel preferentially binds subsets of vesicles or protein complexes that differ by senescence condition independent of membrane integrity (false positive/negative identity calls).

Co‑purified non-vesicular material: soluble SASP components or protein/RNA complexes from SASP-rich samples co-elute with particle peaks and produce capture signal that is detergent/protease-resistant in some assays, confounding membrane-protection interpretation (misclassify non-EV signals as membrane-protected or vice versa).

Formulation/device and administration confounds: intranasal dosing technique, formulation viscosity, droplet size, or mucociliary clearance rates dominate short-interval recoverability differences across samples, producing artifactual group differences unrelated to particle integrity.

Species and scale mismatch: rodent short-interval recoverability positive controls may not translate to primates/humans (ev-driedonks-2022-macaque-biodistribution), so an effect seen in rodents could be non-predictive for clinical delivery risk.

Donor heterogeneity and culture artifacts: within-donor induction of replicative versus induced senescence may not be reproducible, or donor genetics/media differences drive observed EV signatures rather than the intended senescence mechanism.

Detergent/protease assay misinterpretation: incomplete membrane disruption or protease access issues lead to ambiguous protection results, preventing clear classification of membrane‑protected versus soluble material.
Insufficient biological replicates: observed differences do not reproduce across ≥3 donor-matched preparations, leaving the hypothesis underpowered and unresolvable.

Overfitting to orthogonal signature: defining a go/no-go gate on a narrowly chosen orthogonal readout that is highly assay-dependent could cause inappropriate lot rejection or false security if that readout does not correlate with potency or in vivo delivery in relevant species.
strongest_objection: The proposed experiment may conflate assay and administration limits with a true biological effect of senescence mechanism: existing large-animal data show intranasal EVs can be retained in the nose and not reach CSF/brain (ev-driedonks-2022-macaque-biodistribution), and MI SEV guidance warns that EV separation/labeling/capture methods and non-vesicular co‑purified material frequently drive apparent differences (ev-misev2023-quality-framework). Therefore a null or discordant in vivo recovery result could reflect insufficient assay sensitivity, spike-in incompatibility, formulation/device-driven mucociliary clearance, or labeling/processing artifacts rather than any senescence‑mechanism effect—making the causal inference (senescence mechanism → altered membrane protection and nasal→CNS recoverability) unmeasurable or misleading without additional controls and orthogonal in vivo delivery validation. Rodent efficacy/biodistribution reports (ev-hermann-2023-neonatal-hi) support feasibility in small animals but do not resolve whether senescence mechanism or other source/process variables (donor, media, fractionation, device) explain differences, so relying on short-interval rodent recovery alone risks overinterpreting species- and assay-limited signals.
